title: bispectrum: Selective G-Bispectra Made Practical
claim: The library covers a unified set of group actions, spanning finite groups and continuous domains, each shown with its symmetry and domain.
layout: 1 row, 7 icons in 2 grouped headers, orange dot marks a point
description: A single horizontal strip of seven black line icons, split under two bold headers: 'Finite groups' on the left (3 items) and 'Continuous domains' on the right (4 items). The finite items are Cyclic (ring of dots), Dihedral (hexagon with a dashed mirror axis) and Octahedral (octahedron). The continuous items are Circle, Torus (square with arrows on the edges), Disk (concentric rings) and Sphere (globe). Each icon has an orange dot marking a point on the domain, to show where a group element acts. Below each icon is a name label and a math line, such as C_n ↷ C_n, SO(2) ↷ S^1 or SO(3) ↷ S^2, giving the group action. The figure is monochrome with orange accents and has no arrows or flow.
caption: The seven group actions G ↷X (group G acting on domain X) in bispectrum.
abstract: Many machine learning tasks are invariant under transformations such as translations and rotations. The $G$-bispectrum is a complete invariant that determines a signal up to a group action, but its computation is costly and existing implementations each cover a single group. We present bispectrum, an open-source, fully unit-tested PyTorch library providing efficient, differentiable selective $G$-bispectra for seven group actions. Selectivity reduces the number of coefficients from $O(|G|^2)$ to $O(|G|)$ for finite groups, from $O(m^{5/2})$ to $O(m)$ for planar rotations on the disk with $m$ harmonics, and from $Î(L^3)$ to $Î(L^2)$ for spherical 3D rotations using our augmented selective spherical bispectrum at band limit $L$. The library is invariant up to floating-point error and computes selective $G$-bispectra in sub-millisecond time on GPU. We evaluate them as pooling layers on PatchCamelyon and OrganMNIST3D against five baselines. Across 46 comparisons, bispectral pooling remains competitive, matching all baselines on PCam and improving on max pooling by 5.0 percentage points on OrganMNIST3D. On Spherical MNIST, our method with an MLP head reaches 95.8% on rotated test digits, matching a spherical CNN at $4\times$ lower latency and coming within 0.3 percentage points of a tensor-product network at $364\times$ lower latency. Selective $G$-bispectra provide fast, competitive invariant layers for finite and continuous groups.
